[Next unit: Lineage, replay, redaction, retention, and integrations →](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-lineage-replay-redaction-retention-and-integrations/)


================================================================================
CHAPTER: Lineage, replay, redaction, retention, and integrations
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-lineage-replay-redaction-retention-and-integrations/
SUMMARY: Connect versioned evidence to observed runs, distinguish replay from live execution, and design selective telemetry with explicit retention.
================================================================================

# Lineage, replay, redaction, retention, and integrations

## Why this matters

This optional deep dive builds on [events, traces, metrics and correlation](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-events-traces-metrics-and-correlation/). It answers a practical question: after finding an unusual run, what evidence can you still inspect or replay? Readers staying on the main path can continue to [evaluation and benchmarks](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/chapter-plan.md).

### Learning objectives

- Link observed actions to versioned inputs and artifacts.
- Separate inspection, mocked replay and new live execution.
- Explain how content selection, storage and retention shape reconstruction.

## How it works

**Lineage** records where an artifact came from and which observed inputs or operations produced it. A shop answer might reference a catalog version, a retrieval result, the stock tool version and an output artifact. Attach those references to the run and span identifiers from the previous chapter.

In this guide's design, lineage includes the application version, configured model identifier, prompt-template version and source snapshot reference. These fields help compare runs. A model name alone does not freeze a hosted service's behavior. A reference does not guarantee that the referenced content remains available, and a content digest identifies bytes without explaining why the model chose an answer.

**Replay** needs a precise mode:

| Mode | What happens | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trace playback | Display recorded events and timings | Retained telemetry |
| Mocked replay | Recompute a chosen application step with recorded results replacing services | Step code, configuration and suitable fixtures |
| Live rerun | Execute a fresh run with current services | New authorization and current execution conditions |

These are design categories used in this chapter. A replay label should say which mode ran. Showing a timeline does not reproduce execution. Even identical visible inputs may yield different model outputs or encounter changed inventory on a live rerun.

A **checkpoint** saves execution state so a runtime can continue. LangGraph uses checkpointers for thread state and stores for data across threads. A telemetry trace has a different purpose and may lack the state needed to resume. Consult the runtime's persistence contract before using saved state to continue work. [Persistence](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence).

## Data flow and state changes

![Cartoon robot selecting telemetry fields before collection, with retained records feeding a dashboard and optional replay fixtures kept separately](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/11-observability-and-tracing/02-lineage-replay-redaction-retention-and-integrations/01-concept.webp)

*Figure 1. Select content before delivery, then manage telemetry and replay fixtures as distinct stores.*

Instrumentation emits records. An application selects allowed fields and removes unsuitable content. A **collector** receives telemetry, processes it and passes it to an **exporter**, which sends it to a destination. OpenTelemetry configures receivers, processors and exporters in enabled pipelines; processor order determines transformation order. [Collector configuration](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/configuration/).

The diagram's dashboard reads retained telemetry. Its offline replay reader also needs suitable fixtures, kept separately when the application chooses to retain them. Both paths preserve references, but neither assumes that every prompt exists in the telemetry store.

**Redaction** removes or masks content. Prefer collecting only fields needed for a stated debugging question. Review nested attributes, errors and automatically captured library fields as well as top-level prompts. Hashing predictable user identifiers can still permit matching or guessing. [Handling sensitive data](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/security/handling-sensitive-data/).

**Retention** defines how long a store keeps data. Give telemetry and fixtures explicit lifetimes and deletion behavior. Expiring a reference does not delete its target; deleting an active record does not automatically remove exported copies or backups. In this example, a 60-second lifetime makes expiry easy to test. It is an illustrative value, not a recommended production period.

## Worked example

The shop run records `run-1`, a successful outcome, version labels and `fixture-1`. Its ordinary telemetry excludes the prompt, headers and nested error text. A separate synthetic fixture contains a stock count of four.

The offline reader can reproduce the small summary step using that fixture. If the fixture is missing, it reports that replay is unavailable. It never silently substitutes a live stock lookup. Once the telemetry record expires, the local retained list no longer includes it.

## Minimal implementation

Run the [offline example](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/11-observability-and-tracing/02-lineage-replay-redaction-retention-and-integrations/main.py). It uses the standard library, synthetic records and a local list instead of an exporter backend.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
def export_record(raw, destination):
    selected = select_record(raw)
    destination.append(selected)
```

</details>

The full example checks unknown-field removal, rejection before delivery, available and missing replay fixtures, and the exact expiry boundary. The allowlist accepts only this demo's application-generated references. General systems need validation for every allowed field. The list filter models active-record expiry; it does not implement deletion across storage systems.

## Framework implementations

| Integration | Role | Check before connecting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenTelemetry pipeline | Transport and transform cross-service signals | Enabled components, processor order and destination schema |
| OpenAI Agents SDK tracing | Capture framework operations and notify processors | Content settings, processor destinations and field mapping |

The SDK's `trace_include_sensitive_data` defaults to true in the referenced documentation. Set it explicitly for the intended content policy and inspect custom fields. `add_trace_processor()` adds another observer while retaining existing processors; `set_trace_processors()` replaces them. A redaction observer that fails does not stop independent exporters. When delivery depends on redaction, keep selection and delivery in one application-owned exporter, configured before traces are created. [SDK tracing](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/).

## Limitations and trade-offs

Sampling, which retains only selected telemetry, reduces the available reconstruction evidence. So do missing instrumentation and expired fixtures. Mark such gaps instead of treating an incomplete trace as a complete account. Minimal content improves control over collection but can limit later debugging. Decide which question each retained field answers.

## Security preview

A live rerun can create fresh side effects. Apply current [human oversight](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/10-human-in-the-loop/chapter-plan.md), authorization and tool confirmation rules. Later [observability security](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/07-security-by-component-and-workflow-stage/05-human-interfaces-and-observability/chapter-plan.md) examines exposure and detection in more detail.

## Key takeaways

- Lineage connects observed operations, versions and artifacts.
- Trace playback, mocked replay and live reruns need different evidence.
- Redaction and delivery must follow the same intended content policy.
- Retention determines which reconstruction questions remain answerable.

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

Can trace playback recreate a deleted tool fixture? No. Playback shows retained telemetry; mocked replay needs suitable retained inputs and results.

</details>

## References

- OpenTelemetry. [Handling sensitive data](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/security/handling-sensitive-data/) and [Collector configuration](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/configuration/).
- OpenAI. [Agents SDK tracing](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/).
- LangChain. [LangGraph persistence](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence).

Return to [main-path tracing](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-events-traces-metrics-and-correlation/), or continue to [evaluation](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/chapter-plan.md).

================================================================================
CHAPTER: Evaluation levels, test design, and metrics
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-evaluation-levels-test-design-and-metrics/
SUMMARY: Measure components, observed steps, actual outcomes and repeated-run reliability using explicit acceptance rules.
================================================================================

# Evaluation levels, test design, and metrics

## Why this matters

Lee asks the shop assistant to reserve two blue mugs. It calls the stock tool correctly, writes a convincing reply and ends without an error. But the reservation database contains no reservation. A healthy trace tells us that software ran; it does not establish that Lee's goal was met.

**Evaluation** means checking behavior against stated expectations. Begin with the task: which mugs, how many, for whom, and what should happen if stock is unavailable? The [observability records](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/11-observability-and-tracing/chapter-plan.md) supply evidence; acceptance rules decide what that evidence means.

## How it works

### Turn a request into a test case

A **test case** specifies an input, starting conditions and acceptance rules. A **test set** collects cases. An **environment** contains the tools and state in which the agent acts. A **simulator** imitates part of that environment, such as a customer or stock service. Each fresh attempt is a **trial**.

An **oracle** is the reference used to decide correctness: for example, an expected reservation record. An **evaluator**, also called a grader, applies checks. A **metric** summarizes a measurement, such as the proportion of trials that pass. A **benchmark** packages tasks and an evaluation procedure so results can be compared under stated conditions. These are different jobs, even when one script performs several of them.

For our shop, restore stock to three mugs before each trial. Ask for two. Require one reservation for exactly two mugs and remaining stock of one. Also include insufficient stock, ambiguous color, a failed lookup and interruption before the write. A correct clarification or failure report can be the expected outcome of a case.

Keep the task understandable to both the agent and reviewer. Do not grade an unstated requirement. Check that a known valid solution passes and a known wrong solution fails. Isolate trial state, including files and durable memories, unless persistence is deliberately part of the test. [Agent evaluation guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

### Choose the level that answers your question

These four levels are a teaching map, not a prescribed architecture:

| Level | Shop question | Useful measurement | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Component | Did the tool receive a valid quantity? | Argument validity, lookup accuracy | Whether a reservation exists |
| Trajectory | Did the assistant read evidence before acting? | Required observations, unnecessary calls | Whether the final write worked |
| Task | Is the requested reservation present? | Verified task pass or failure | Reliability across other requests |
| System | Does the service keep working across tasks and runs? | Failure rate, time, cost, recovery | Behavior outside the sampled conditions |

A **trajectory** is the observed sequence of messages, calls and results. It is not access to hidden model reasoning. ADK exposes trajectory and response evaluation separately. An exact tool sequence is useful when order is required, but a broader condition can allow equivalent valid routes. [ADK evaluation](https://adk.dev/evaluate/).

![Four illustrated levels connect valid tool arguments, necessary observed steps, a verified shop reservation and repeated trials with time and cost.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/01-evaluation-levels-test-design-and-metrics/01-evaluation-stack.webp)

*Figure 1. Read from a local check toward the whole service. A success at one shelf does not automatically pass the next shelf. The task shelf checks the shop's records, rather than the robot's claim. Numbers and item IDs in the illustration are invented examples, separate from the blue-mug trial below; they are not measured performance.*

### Use the right kind of grader

A deterministic check applies a fixed rule, such as comparing database fields. A **judge model** scores an answer using a **rubric**, an explicit set of criteria. Human review can resolve ambiguous cases and check whether the rubric represents the intended task.

For the shop, code verifies stock and reservations; a reviewer assesses whether the explanation is clear. A judge's favorable wording score cannot replace a missing reservation. Calibrate model judgments against human-reviewed examples, including wrong answers that sound persuasive, and permit an unknown result when evidence is missing. [Grader guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

### Repeat trials and keep the denominators visible

**Pass rate** is passed trials divided by attempted trials under a defined rule. **Variance** describes how measurements spread across runs or cases. Report case counts, attempts per case and failed or ungraded attempts, alongside the score. Do not quietly remove timeouts from the denominator.

**pass@k** asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds. **pass^k** asks whether all k attempts succeed. If independent attempts on one task each succeed with probability p, these probabilities are 1 - (1 - p)^k and p^k respectively. These are explanatory formulas under an independence assumption, not automatic estimators for every dataset. For heterogeneous tasks, compute the per-task quantity before averaging; a shared outage or retained state can break independence. τ-bench introduced pass^k to expose inconsistency across repeated tool-user interactions. [τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045).

For an illustrative p = 0.8 and k = 3, at least one success is 99.2%, while all three successes is 51.2%. Neither number means users can obtain a verified reservation 99.2% of the time in one interaction. Retrying also requires a way to detect failure and avoid duplicate effects.

### Compare complete configurations

Record the model version, agent harness, tool schemas, instructions or skill versions, environment snapshot, memory policy, budgets and grader version. The **agent harness** is the code that runs the model and tools. The **evaluation harness** runs the tests and grading. Changes to either can change a result.

Measure end-to-end elapsed time, including waits, and state whether human waiting is included. Report the median, the middle value of ordered measurements, and a tail percentile, such as the 95th percentile, a value at or below which roughly 95% of observations fall. Include enough observations to interpret these measurements. Count model and tool costs for failed trials too. Cost per verified success is total trial cost divided by verified successes; with none, report that it is undefined. Compare direct tool loops and code orchestration on the same cases and budgets. These are our reporting conventions, not provider guarantees.

## Worked example

The [offline grader](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/01-evaluation-levels-test-design-and-metrics/README.md) simulates four scripts against fresh shop state. It checks final records separately from required observations. One script says "Reserved" without writing anything. Another writes correctly but skips the required lookup. Both distinctions appear in the output.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
outcome_ok = reservations == [{"sku": "blue-mug", "quantity": 2}]
trajectory_ok = "read_stock" in observed_steps
accepted = outcome_ok and trajectory_ok
```

The runnable example also checks remaining stock. Its required lookup is a stated condition of this teaching task, not a rule that every reservation workflow must use that exact call. No model is invoked; scripted cases demonstrate the grader, not model capability.

</details>

## Limitations and trade-offs

Mocks make failures repeatable but may omit real tool behavior, user ambiguity or changing data. A large score on a narrow test set is evidence about that set. Review failures by category, compare representative tasks and include interrupted work with recovery. Detailed benchmark and release practice follows in the optional [deep dive](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-benchmarks-regression-and-release-evaluation/). To stay on the main path, continue to [multi-agent systems](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/).

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

A judge rates the reply highly and all tool calls returned successfully. The reservation table is empty. Should the reservation task pass?

No. Those checks measure communication and execution. The stated task requires an actual reservation. Investigate whether the tool result was misunderstood, the write was omitted or the outcome check is looking at the wrong state.

</details>

## Security preview

Functional evaluations show whether intended tasks work. They do not establish resistance to hostile inputs. Pass 2 adds [security testing and assurance](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/09-security-testing-evaluation-and-assurance/chapter-plan.md) with explicit threat assumptions and separate checks.

## Key takeaways

- State success before choosing metrics, and check actual artifacts or external state.
- Measure components, observed trajectories, tasks and repeated service behavior separately.
- Report complete configurations, denominators, uncertainty, latency and cost.
- A repeatable simulator and a calibrated grader are useful evidence with visible limits.

## References

- [τ-bench: Tool-Agent-User Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045).
- [ADK: Why evaluate agents](https://adk.dev/evaluate/).
- [Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

[Next unit: Benchmarks, regression, and release evaluation →](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-benchmarks-regression-and-release-evaluation/)


================================================================================
CHAPTER: Benchmarks, regression, and release evaluation
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-benchmarks-regression-and-release-evaluation/
SUMMARY: Use benchmark results as scoped evidence and test candidate releases against retained behaviors, new cases and operational budgets.
================================================================================

# Benchmarks, regression, and release evaluation

## Why this matters

Lee's new assistant answers product questions better, but now fails an old cancellation case. Its overall score improved because most test cases ask product questions. Lee still needs to know whether replacing the existing assistant is a good decision.

This deep dive follows the [evaluation levels](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-evaluation-levels-test-design-and-metrics/). A benchmark measures performance under its procedure. A **regression** is a loss of behavior that previously worked. A release decision connects both to the service's actual requirements.

## How it works

### Ask what the benchmark actually measures

A benchmark result belongs to a task distribution, environment, grader and agent configuration. Match those to your use case before interpreting a score.

| Primary benchmark | What it exercises | What Lee still needs to test locally |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [AgentBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03688) | Decisions in eight interactive environments | Shop-specific tasks, tool failures and recovery |
| [GAIA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12983) | Questions combining reasoning, browsing, tools and multimodal input | Whether reservations and cancellations change the correct records |
| [SWE-bench](https://www.swebench.com/SWE-bench/guides/evaluation/) | Patches applied to repositories and graded by tests | Shop behavior; software tests cover only their assertions |
| [τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045) | Simulated customer interactions, policies, tools and final database states | Actual customer behavior and deployed tool semantics |

These are examples of benchmark designs, not a current ranking. A browser-dependent question may change when its page changes. A simulated user can omit the pauses, mistakes or corrections real customers make. Passing a coding benchmark does not directly measure reservation-service quality.

The 2026 [Harness-Bench preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27922) compares model-harness pairings under shared offline tasks and budgets, examining artifacts, traces and resource use. Its lesson for this guide is a bounded reporting practice: name the configuration you evaluated. Do not assign the whole system's score to its base model alone.

### Give datasets different jobs

**Development cases** guide changes to prompts, tools or skills. **Held-out cases** are kept out of those tuning decisions. A **regression set** retains behaviors the product must keep. A **capability set** probes new or difficult work. One case can be relevant to several purposes, but repeated inspection of its answer means it is no longer untouched evidence of generalization.

**Contamination** occurs when evaluation information enters training or tuning in a way that weakens the intended test. It can involve benchmark answers in model training, or a developer repeatedly optimizing a prompt against a supposedly held-out set. Exact text matching is insufficient to exclude all leakage; rephrased samples can still distort results. [Rephrased-sample contamination research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04850).

Our shop convention is to tune on development cases, use a separate retained regression suite, and reserve fresh cases for final comparison. Split related requests by scenario family when paraphrases share the same answer. Keep reviewer notes and grader access separate from the inputs provided to the agent. If final results inform another change, document that reuse and obtain new held-out evidence where needed.

### Make comparisons fair and inspectable

Run baseline and candidate against the same case IDs, starting snapshots and budgets. Pair results by case; record which cases improved and which regressed. Repeat trials because one run can be lucky. Inspect [traces and lineage](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/11-observability-and-tracing/chapter-plan.md) to separate task failure, tool failure and a broken evaluation environment.

Record model, harness, tool, prompt, skill, memory and evaluator versions. Include timeouts, missing outputs and interrupted runs. Report outcome pass rates alongside latency and total cost. A one-case improvement in a tiny set is not strong evidence of a durable gain; uncertainty should reflect task sampling as well as repeated runs.

Some evaluation harnesses cache results. SWE-bench documents that reuse of the same run and instance identifiers can reuse prior results even when a patch changes. A fresh configuration comparison needs appropriate run identifiers and verified artifacts. A completed harness operation also differs from a resolved issue. [SWE-bench evaluation guide](https://www.swebench.com/SWE-bench/guides/evaluation/).

### Define the release decision before seeing the scores

A **release gate** is a stated acceptance rule for a candidate. The following is an illustrative shop policy, not an industry threshold:

| Requirement | Evidence checked | Decision on failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain mandatory cancellation and reservation cases | Per-case outcomes over repeated trials | Hold the candidate and inspect the failure |
| Improve new product-question cases | Baseline and candidate on fresh cases | Seek more evidence if the difference is uncertain |
| Remain within time and cost budgets | End-to-end measurements including failed trials | Adjust the design or decline the release |
| Preserve interrupted-work recovery | Verified external records after resume | Fix recovery before release |

Do not hide a mandatory failure inside an aggregate score. Also avoid pretending that zero failures in a finite sample proves a zero failure rate. A team can set stricter rules for high-impact tasks and accept a documented trade-off for optional behaviors.

![A robot presents three separate evidence folders for new tasks, retained behaviors and time and cost to a reviewer deciding release or hold.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/02-benchmarks-regression-and-release-evaluation/01-release-evidence.webp)

*Figure 1. Read each evidence folder before the decision. A better new-task score cannot erase a failed required behavior. The reviewer owns the release decision; the folders supply evidence.*

## Worked example

The [offline release comparison](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/02-benchmarks-regression-and-release-evaluation/README.md) uses invented outcomes. Both configurations pass reservation cases. The candidate improves product answers but loses one cancellation trial. Its aggregate pass rate is higher, yet the mandatory regression rule holds the release. A missing case also holds it.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
regressions = [case for case in required_cases
               if not all(candidate_results[case])]
release = not regressions
```

The runnable version checks that expected case IDs are present and trial counts match, and applies an illustrative cost budget. It evaluates supplied records; it does not run a model or provide statistical confidence from this small fixture.

</details>

## Limitations and trade-offs

A frozen suite protects known behaviors but can miss new usage. Add cases from reviewed failures, keeping personal data out of teaching fixtures. Preserve the old suite and configuration so you can explain score changes after grading updates. Beyond the offline gate, observe a controlled rollout, define when to restore the earlier configuration and reconcile any external actions already taken. Changing a deployment version does not undo those actions.

The next main-path section covers [multi-agent systems](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/chapter-plan.md), where coordination creates additional trajectories and failure categories to evaluate.

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

The candidate gains ten product-answer successes and loses one mandatory cancellation case. Its overall score rises. Is that enough to release it?

No. Check the predeclared gate and repeat the disputed case to understand the failure. A higher aggregate measures a different trade-off from preserving mandatory behavior. Record the uncertainty and decision rather than silently changing the gate after seeing the result.

</details>

## Security preview

Functional regression suites do not replace [security testing and assurance](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/09-security-testing-evaluation-and-assurance/chapter-plan.md). Pass 2 adds hostile scenarios and tests for component boundaries using separate acceptance rules.

## Key takeaways

- Compare benchmark designs and configurations, not isolated leaderboard numbers.
- Keep tuning, retained behavior checks and fresh evaluation evidence distinct.
- Use per-case regressions, operational budgets and explicit release rules.
- Keep the environment, grader and result provenance visible when scores change.

## References

- [AgentBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03688), [GAIA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12983), [τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045).
- [SWE-bench evaluation guide](https://www.swebench.com/SWE-bench/guides/evaluation/).
- [Harness-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27922), May 2026 preprint.
- [Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination with Rephrased Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04850).

[Next unit: Multi-agent roles, delegation, and coordination →](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/)


================================================================================
CHAPTER: Multi-agent roles, delegation, and coordination
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/
SUMMARY: Decide who owns the reply, what specialists receive and return, and how team work stops before adding agents.
================================================================================

# Multi-agent roles, delegation, and coordination

## Why this matters

Lee wants a report on which products need restocking and whether suppliers can deliver them this week. The assistant could handle both lookups itself. A team becomes useful only if separating stock analysis from supplier research makes the task clearer or performs better under the same evaluation conditions.

A **multi-agent system** contains multiple agent instances that coordinate work. A **role** describes an instance's job; a **specialist** has a narrower job, context or tool set. Different roles can use the same model. Naming two prompts "agents" does not by itself create useful cooperation.

Start with a single-agent **baseline**, a reference configuration for comparison. Add a specialist for a concrete reason, such as a separate tool contract or an independent research subtask, then measure the result. AutoGen also recommends trying an adequately equipped single agent before adopting a team. [AutoGen teams](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/teams.html).

## How it works

### First decide who owns the answer

**Delegation** assigns a bounded piece of work. In an **agent-as-tool** pattern, the caller invokes a specialist and receives a result, much like any other tool. A **manager**, also called a supervisor, remains responsible for combining results and responding to the user.

A **handoff** transfers active conversation control to another agent. The receiving specialist owns the next response for that branch. This differs from calling a helper and waiting for its return. OpenAI's Agents SDK exposes both patterns: Python `Agent.as_tool()` wraps a specialist as a callable capability, while `handoffs` specifies agents that may take over. These are SDK mechanisms, not permission grants. [OpenAI orchestration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/orchestration).

In Lee's report, stock and supplier specialists return evidence to a manager. If Lee instead asks a billing question, a router could hand the conversation to billing, which asks any needed follow-up itself. **Routing** selects the destination; it need not be another model call. Fixed code can route a known category.

![Two cartoon scenes contrast a manager receiving specialist reports and keeping the user reply with a router handing the conversation to a specialist.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/01-delegation-and-handoff.webp)

*Figure 1. In the upper scene, reports return to the manager. In the lower scene, the conversation moves to a specialist. Follow the owner of the user reply, rather than merely counting robots.*

### Choose coordination to match the task

A **peer** communicates with other agents without one agent serving as permanent manager. A **team** is the participating agents plus the coordination rules. A **blackboard** is a shared task or evidence store that workers inspect and update. **Consensus** is agreement under a declared rule; agreement does not make a factual claim correct.

The following are design patterns, not mutually exclusive product categories:

| Pattern | Control and message flow | State and action ownership | Failure and stopping rule in a concrete design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Supervisor-worker | Manager delegates; workers return results | Manager owns task record and final reply; workers have bounded tools | Manager detects missing results, applies deadline and checks acceptance |
| Router-specialist | Router chooses one branch; specialist continues | Chosen specialist owns conversation state and permitted branch actions | Unknown category falls back; handoff count and task budget are bounded |
| Sequential team | Each stage passes its result to the next | Runtime owns stage state; each stage writes its artifact | Missing required output stops downstream work |
| Concurrent team | Independent subtasks run together; collector joins results | Workers keep local context; collector owns combined result | Join records partial failures and cancels unneeded work |
| Blackboard | Workers claim tasks and publish evidence on a board | Store owns task state; writes need explicit conflict rules | Claims expire or are reassigned; finish only when required tasks are accepted |
| Group chat or debate | Participants discuss; a scheduler chooses turns | Shared messages provide context; a designated actor performs external writes | Bound rounds and decide with evidence, not endless discussion |
| Peer-to-peer or event-driven team | Peers send messages or react to recorded events | Local state plus shared identifiers; each action has a named owner | Detect missing, duplicate or cyclic work; apply deadlines and completion checks |

Semantic Kernel documents concurrent, sequential, handoff, group-chat and Magentic orchestrations, while marking this feature experimental. AutoGen's round-robin team schedules turns; its selector team uses a model to choose a speaker. A group conversation is therefore not necessarily simultaneous execution. [Semantic Kernel orchestration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/semantic-kernel/frameworks/agent/agent-orchestration/) and [AutoGen teams](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/teams.html).

### Make each assignment a small contract

For the shop, the manager gives stock analysis the product IDs, inventory snapshot, question, result format and budget. Supplier research receives only the products needing stock and the delivery window. Neither receives an instruction to place an order.

Each request and response carries a task ID, parent task ID, sender, recipient and attempt identifier. The request states scope, allowed tools, expected evidence, deadline and completion rule. The response distinguishes success, partial evidence, failure and a need for clarification. It includes artifact references and unresolved assumptions, rather than only a polished summary.

**Shared context** is information shown to multiple agents. **Shared state** is a durable record that more than one participant may read or change. They are not equivalent: two specialists can receive the same old inventory snapshot without seeing each other's updates. Link task IDs to the existing [trace records](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/11-observability-and-tracing/chapter-plan.md).

A role such as "buyer" is descriptive. [Identity and authorization](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/08-identity-authorization-and-secrets/chapter-plan.md) determine whether its actual tool credentials can place an order. Delegating analysis does not automatically delegate the caller's permissions. A team's state and messaging design must preserve that distinction.

### Bound the delegation chain

A worker may delegate a smaller subtask, creating a parent-child chain. Give that chain a total call, time and cost budget, not merely a fresh unlimited budget at every child. Set a maximum depth and decide which failures propagate to the parent. These are shop application rules, not automatic guarantees of an agent framework.

![A manager delegates through a supplier specialist to a delivery helper, with one shared time and cost budget and a depth limit on further delegation.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/02-bounded-delegation-chain.webp)

*Figure 2. Task envelopes move outward; evidence returns to the caller. The shared budget spans every participant. A new helper does not reset that budget, and the depth limit stops another level of delegation.*

Define **termination**, the condition that stops work. A manager may stop after required evidence is accepted, after a deadline, or when Lee cancels. Record the reason. A timeout ends computation under the runtime's cancellation behavior; it does not prove that already-issued external actions were undone. The optional [coordination deep dive](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-shared-state-failures-termination-and-evaluation/) examines these cases.

## Worked example

In the [offline manager-specialist example](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/README.md), a stock specialist returns low-stock IDs. A supplier specialist returns delivery evidence. The manager joins them and owns the answer. Missing supplier evidence produces a partial result, and nobody places an order.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
stock_result = stock_specialist(inventory_snapshot)
delivery_result = supplier_specialist(stock_result.low_stock)
answer = manager_combine(stock_result, delivery_result)
```

The runnable version uses fixed Python functions to expose contracts. It is a simulation of orchestration; there are no model calls or claims that multiple agents improve performance.

</details>

## Framework implementations

Map the ownership contract before choosing framework APIs:

| Framework | How the shop design maps | Boundary to keep explicit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | Manager calls specialists through `as_tool()`; conversation transfer uses `handoffs` | Reply ownership and supplied history are distinct from external service permissions |
| AutoGen AgentChat | Teams coordinate participants; selectors or fixed turn order choose who responds | A team message is not a durable inventory transaction |
| Semantic Kernel | Sequential or concurrent orchestration passes or collects outputs; handoff changes active agent | Experimental APIs and runtime behavior require version checks |

These mappings were checked against the linked documentation on October 14, 2026. They are conceptual translations; the offline example does not install these SDKs.

## Limitations and trade-offs

More agents add calls, message volume and coordination work. Parallelism helps only when work is sufficiently independent; a dependency on fresh stock keeps supplier work sequential here. Two agents can repeat the same mistake, especially when they use the same model and evidence. Debate and consensus need outcome verification too.

Evaluate against the single-agent baseline using [the same cases and budgets](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/chapter-plan.md). Track final outcomes, missing handoffs, duplicate work, total calls and combined cost. Improvements in local worker answers do not guarantee a better combined report.

To stay on the main path, continue to the [learning section](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/), which separates changes to team instructions or skills from model training.

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

A supplier agent returns delivery dates to the manager, which writes the final report. Was that a handoff?

No. It was bounded delegation using an agent as a tool. A handoff would transfer the active conversation so the supplier agent owns the next user-facing response. In either case, ordering stock still requires a separately permitted action.

</details>

## Security preview

Each transfer introduces another component that receives information and may request actions. Pass 2 maps cascading trust and cross-agent risks to [multi-agent and protocol security](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/07-security-by-component-and-workflow-stage/06-multi-agent-and-protocols/chapter-plan.md).

## Key takeaways

- Add agents for a measured reason and retain a single-agent baseline.
- Agent-as-tool delegation returns a result; handoff changes conversation ownership.
- Define message, state, action, failure and stopping contracts for every pattern.
- Shared messages and agreement do not establish current state or factual truth.

## References

- [OpenAI: Orchestration and handoffs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/orchestration).
- [AutoGen: Teams](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/teams.html).
- [Semantic Kernel: Agent Orchestration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/semantic-kernel/frameworks/agent/agent-orchestration/).

[Next unit: Shared state, failures, termination, and evaluation →](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-shared-state-failures-termination-and-evaluation/)


================================================================================
CHAPTER: Shared state, failures, termination, and evaluation
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/02-shared-state-failures-termination-and-evaluation/
SUMMARY: Track task ownership, reject stale results and separate accepted outcomes from the reasons a multi-agent run stops.
================================================================================

# Shared state, failures, termination, and evaluation

## Why this matters

Two shop agents see that blue mugs need restocking. Both prepare an order. Their conversation sounds cooperative, yet the shop could receive twice the intended quantity. Another worker finishes after its task has been reassigned and overwrites the newer answer.

This deep dive builds on [roles and delegation](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-multi-agent-roles-delegation-and-coordination/). It explains how a team records ownership and progress. Readers returning to the main path can continue to [learning and adaptation](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/chapter-plan.md).

## How it works

### Separate messages from the task record

A message is evidence that a participant said or returned something. The **task record** states the system's current accepted view: task ID, parent, required dependencies, owner, attempt, status, deadline and artifact reference. An **artifact** is an output such as a report or a file. A final sentence saying "done" is not the task record.

Two participants can hold different context histories even when they read the same shared board. A **stale read** uses an older value. A **conflicting write** changes state based on an assumption that another participant has already changed. A **lost update** overwrites another accepted change.

For our shop, peers can prepare independent evidence, but only a designated component commits an order. Inventory and order creation need the store's concurrency rules. Database transaction isolation describes which concurrent effects are permitted; PostgreSQL's stronger isolation modes can require retrying the whole transaction after a serialization failure. That guarantee covers the database transaction, not every remote tool in the workflow. [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html).

### Give a claim an owner and an expiry

A **claim** assigns a task to a worker. A **lease** is a claim valid until a specified time. If the worker stops responding, another worker can take the task after expiry. Our teaching board issues an increasing **generation number** with each reassignment. Submitted results must match the current owner and generation.

Suppose stock analysis generation 1 belongs to peer A until time 5. At time 5, peer B claims generation 2. A late result from A must not replace B's output. Check ownership and generation as part of the same state change that stores the result. Checking first and writing later in separate operations leaves a race, a timing window in which ownership can change.

A generation check protects the board only where it is enforced. It does not stop an old worker from calling an external service that ignores that generation. Action ownership, cancellation and retry behavior must still match [the execution design](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/09-execution-environments/chapter-plan.md).

### Use explicit states and acceptance

The shop board uses the following states as an application convention:

| State | Meaning | Next decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ready | Dependencies allow the task to begin | A peer may claim it |
| Claimed | One current owner has a valid lease | Collect result, renew claim or reassign after expiry |
| Verifying | A current result exists but has not passed acceptance | Accept it or record why it failed |
| Accepted | Evidence satisfies the task's declared rule | Dependents can use the accepted artifact |
| Failed | The current attempt did not meet its rule | Retry if allowed, otherwise report failure |
| Cancelled | The task has been stopped by request or policy | Reject later results and reconcile external effects |

A task can return to Ready for a permitted new attempt. Keep prior attempts and rejection reasons in its event history. Parent completion requires all mandatory child results to be accepted, not simply that every worker has spoken. An optional child can fail while a report is explicitly partial; that rule must be stated in advance.

![A cartoon task board shows ready, claimed, verifying and accepted states, with an expired claim returning for reassignment and cancelled work kept separate.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/02-shared-state-failures-termination-and-evaluation/01-task-state-and-recovery.webp)

*Figure 1. Follow the normal path toward an accepted artifact. The return path represents a new claim after expiry. The cancellation branch stops accepting work. None of these arrows implies that a remote purchase was reversed.*

### Handle incomplete or repeated messages

A **duplicate** is a repeated delivery of the same message or operation. Record a message ID and the attempt it belongs to. A repeated accepted message should not create a second artifact or action. If the same ID carries different content, treat it as a conflict to investigate. This is a local design rule; it does not promise exactly-once delivery.

A **deadlock** occurs when participants wait on each other without a runnable step. A **livelock** keeps exchanging or revising work without making accepted progress. A circular handoff can create either. Track dependencies, bound handoff depth and detect repeated task destinations or unchanged results. A human review state needs a named reviewer and a resume condition, not a loop asking the same question indefinitely.

When saving and resuming, preserve task ownership, pending work and identifiers alongside agent history. AutoGen documents agent and team `save_state()` and `load_state()` operations. Such snapshots help restore framework state; they do not atomically snapshot all outside services. Before retrying an uncertain write, inspect the external operation's actual status. [AutoGen state](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/state.html).

### Record why the run stopped

A **stop reason** explains termination: accepted required outputs, a message or cost limit, deadline, cancellation, an unresolved failure or a request for human input. Distinguish successful completion from "no more calls will be scheduled".

AutoGen offers message, token, timeout, text, handoff and external stop conditions. A text condition such as detecting "APPROVE" is a scheduling mechanism. It does not independently prove that the output is correct. Keep an outcome check separate from that stop condition. [AutoGen termination](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/termination.html).

Cancellation should stop new scheduling, request cancellation of active work and account for late results. A call already sent may still complete. Store the actual outcome, then report any unresolved effect. Likewise, a budget limit can stop a team safely with a partial report; it must not label the task successful merely because all workers stopped.

## Worked example

The [offline peer-task board](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/13-multi-agent-systems/02-shared-state-failures-termination-and-evaluation/README.md) lets peer A claim a task, then simulates its lease expiry. Peer B reclaims it. The board rejects A's late generation, accepts B's current submission, ignores the same delivered message twice and verifies the artifact before marking it Accepted. A cancellation case rejects a late result too.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
if worker != task.owner or generation != task.generation:
    return "stale result"
if now >= task.lease_until:
    return "expired claim"
```

In the runnable example the check and write happen in one sequential function call. A real shared store needs an atomic update or transaction. No LLM, database or network is used, and no external action is performed.

</details>

## Reliability failures

### Evaluate the coordination, then the outcome

Use the [evaluation levels](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-evaluation-levels-test-design-and-metrics/) for the whole team. The following shop cases exercise distinct failures:

| Case | Coordination observation | Required outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One specialist lacks evidence | Partial result retains the missing dependency | Report does not invent a delivery date |
| Worker expires and returns late | Current generation remains authoritative | Late result cannot replace accepted evidence |
| Message arrives twice | Delivery is recognized as repeated | One artifact or permitted action |
| Peers keep disagreeing | Round budget stops the discussion | Unresolved status remains visible |
| Cancellation during a write | New work stops; issued operation is reconciled | Real external result is reported |
| All workers say done without an artifact | Parent rejects missing evidence | Task is not counted as successful |

The MAST research taxonomy groups sampled failures into system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. It helps organize diagnoses; it does not establish that every failure fits a universal list. [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657).

Compare team and single-agent outcomes under matched budgets. Separate coordinator mistakes from worker mistakes and grader failures. Count total tokens, calls, end-to-end time, duplicate work and unresolved tasks. A team that gets better individual answers but fails the join may perform worse for Lee.

## Limitations and trade-offs

A shared board makes coordination inspectable but adds a service and consistency rules. Leases need a defined clock and renewal behavior. Stricter acceptance can delay work while avoiding unsupported completion. Agreement between same-model peers may reflect shared blind spots, so consensus needs independent evidence or a task-specific oracle.

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

Peer A's lease expired and peer B now owns the task. A later sends a correct-looking result with generation 1. Can the board accept it just because its content seems good?

No. Accepting it as the current result would violate the ownership contract and may overwrite newer evidence. Keep it as historical evidence if useful, then verify a result under the current generation. Its arrival also does not prove A's external actions were cancelled.

</details>

## Security preview

This chapter handles ordinary coordination failures. Pass 2 examines deliberately misleading cross-agent messages and state manipulation in [multi-agent and protocol security](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/07-security-by-component-and-workflow-stage/06-multi-agent-and-protocols/chapter-plan.md).

## Key takeaways

- Give shared tasks explicit owners, attempts, states and acceptance rules.
- Enforce stale-result checks where state changes, and deduplicate repeated deliveries.
- Stop reasons, successful outcomes and external rollback are separate facts.
- Evaluate the team's combined artifacts and recovery, not just each worker's answer.

## References

- [AutoGen: Termination](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/termination.html).
- [AutoGen: Managing State](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/state.html).
- [PostgreSQL 18: Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html).
- [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657).

[Next unit: Adaptation, reflection, feedback, and skills →](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/)


================================================================================
CHAPTER: Adaptation, reflection, feedback, and skills
URL: https://renatomignone.github.io/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/
SUMMARY: Separate revising a run, retaining experience, authoring reusable skill packages and training model parameters; require evidence for improvement.
================================================================================

# Adaptation, reflection, feedback, and skills

## Why this matters

Lee's assistant reports that a product is available without checking the stock record. A reviewer points out the missing evidence. The assistant revises the report, and the revised answer is correct. Has the model learned a new permanent behavior?

Several different mechanisms could produce that change. The current conversation may contain a correction; a memory record may be saved for future runs; an instruction package may be revised; or a training process may change model parameters. Saying "the agent improved" without naming the mechanism hides what actually happened.

## How it works

### Locate the change

**Adaptation** means adjusting behavior to a task, environment or feedback. **Inference time** is when an existing model produces outputs. **Training** changes learned model parameters, also called **weights**. The following is a teaching taxonomy, not a formal standard:

| Mechanism | What changes | Persistence and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-context adaptation | Current messages, retrieved evidence or instructions shown to the model | Lasts while that information remains in usable context |
| Refinement | The current draft or proposed action | A better artifact does not imply a better next run |
| Memory update | Stored observations, feedback or summaries | Can influence later runs if retrieved; may be wrong or stale |
| Prompt optimization | A selected version of reusable instructions | Persists in application configuration; can overfit the cases used to select it |
| Skill acquisition or package revision | Reusable procedures, code or instruction files | Persists in a library; retrieval, compatibility and testing still matter |
| Weight update | Model parameters through a training method | Changes the trained model; needs a separate training and evaluation process |

A **policy** is a rule or strategy for choosing actions. In application discussions, a policy update may mean changing rules or a prompt. In machine-learning research, it may mean training the action-producing model. Ask which object changed before interpreting the term.

![Three cartoon workspaces show current context and draft changes, durable memory and skill files, and a separate training process that changes model weights.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/01-adaptation-mechanisms.webp)

*Figure 1. Find the changed object. Editing the current notebook or the reusable library can alter behavior without changing the model's weights. The separate training workspace represents a different mechanism.*

### Use feedback to revise a bounded attempt

**Feedback** supplies information about an output or action. It may come from a user, a reviewer, a tool result, an executable test or the model itself. Its usefulness depends on whether it contains correct, relevant evidence.

**Reflection** is an assessment of a previous attempt, often expressed in language. **Refinement** changes the attempt in response. Self-Refine generates a draft, obtains self-feedback and revises it using the same model without further training. That describes the method evaluated in the paper, not a guarantee for every task. [Self-Refine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651).

For the shop, the strongest feedback says: "Your report lacks a stock source. Snapshot S17 shows one blue mug, but the request asks for two." That is more useful than "think harder". The revised report should state the shortage, rather than only become more confident.

A bounded loop drafts, checks, revises and checks again. Stop on an accepted result, a revision budget, unavailable evidence or a need for clarification. Retain the earlier draft so you can detect a revision that makes it worse. A correct final answer is not evidence that every intermediate revision helped.

Model-generated feedback can repeat the generator's mistake. A study of intrinsic self-correction found unreliable correction on its evaluated reasoning tasks without external feedback. Treat it as counterevidence to universal self-improvement claims, with its historical scope visible. [Self-correction study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798).

### Decide what deserves to survive the run

An **experience** is a recorded attempt and its feedback, evidence and outcome. A durable memory can preserve a useful lesson, but storing a reflection does not make that reflection true. Follow [persistent memory lifecycle rules](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/building-blocks/03-persistent-memory-types-and-lifecycle/): record origin, scope, review status, expiry and invalidation conditions.

Reflexion stores textual reflections in an episodic memory buffer to guide later trials, without updating weights. Its title uses "verbal reinforcement learning" for this feedback mechanism. It should not be read as saying that the underlying model receives a parameter update after each conversation. [Reflexion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366).

In our shop design, a failed case can suggest the candidate rule "attach the stock snapshot ID to availability reports". Keep the original incident separately from the general rule. A human or stated review process decides whether it is broadly useful, whether it conflicts with older requirements and when it should expire. Do not copy one customer's stock count into a permanent universal fact.

### Distinguish two meanings of skill

A **skill** is a reusable capability or procedure. In research, skill acquisition can mean deriving and storing behavior from experience. Voyager builds a library of executable code skills in Minecraft, with a curriculum and environment feedback, without parameter fine-tuning. A **curriculum** selects which tasks or challenges the agent tries next. Minecraft results do not establish that the same process works for shop operations. [Voyager](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291).

An **authored skill package** is prepared instruction material that an agent loads. The Agent Skills specification uses a `SKILL.md` file with required `name` and `description` metadata, followed by instructions. Optional `scripts`, `references` and `assets` hold code, detail and resources. **Progressive disclosure** means loading descriptions first, then the chosen instructions and resources when needed. [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification).

The package may be written by a person or generated and reviewed through a workflow. Reading it changes available context; it does not train weights. Package discovery also differs from action permission: the runtime still controls tools and credentials. The specification's optional `allowed-tools` field is experimental and client-dependent; it is not a universal external authorization mechanism.

Version packages and record why a change was made. In the example, `metadata.version` is our chosen version field within the specification's arbitrary metadata map, not a mandatory versioning standard. Keep the previous package and evaluation record so you can restore it.

![A reviewed feedback path moves from a failed shop report through a candidate reusable rule, fresh and retained tests, then a versioned skill library; rejected candidates retain the previous version.](/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/assets/images/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/02-feedback-to-reviewed-skill.webp)

*Figure 2. A single failure proposes a change; it does not promote the change automatically. Test the candidate on new cases and previously supported behavior before updating the reusable library. Preserve the previous version on rejection. Book version labels in the illustration are examples; the runnable candidate below uses version 1.1.*

## Worked example

The [offline refinement example](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/README.md) starts with a report that guesses availability. A deterministic checker identifies a missing source and a quantity mismatch. A mocked refiner reads the snapshot and produces a corrected report within a bounded loop.

A separate candidate package describes a stock-report procedure. Its [versioned record](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/examples/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/01-adaptation-reflection-feedback-and-skills/skill-record.json) names the incident, intended scope, baseline, transfer and retention cases, and previous version. The example demonstrates these records; it does not autonomously rewrite its own code or invoke training.

<details><summary>Expand minimal Python implementation</summary>

```python
for _ in range(max_revisions):
    feedback = check_report(draft, snapshot)
    if not feedback:
        break
    draft = mock_refine(draft, feedback, snapshot)
```

The full script performs a final acceptance check, including when the revision budget is zero. The checker compares evidence fields with the supplied snapshot. Real evaluations would also check whether that snapshot is an appropriate, fresh source.

</details>

## Limitations and trade-offs

### What evidence would establish improvement?

A **baseline** is the earlier configuration used for comparison. **Transfer** asks whether a change helps tasks beyond the incident that suggested it. **Retention** asks whether earlier capabilities still work. Learning-system discussions use **plasticity** for ability to adapt and **catastrophic forgetting** for a substantial loss of earlier learned performance after new learning. Application prompt or package revisions can cause regressions without any weight update.

For this chapter's candidate skill, record all five elements:

| Element | Shop example |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Revised stock-report instructions; weights unchanged |
| Baseline | Earlier rule that guessed availability without a source |
| Transfer test | Unseen product and changed requested quantity |
| Retention test | Out-of-stock case still reports a shortage; missing data remains unknown |
| Rollback | Restore the previous package version and invalidate the candidate selection |

Use [evaluation methods](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/12-evaluation-and-benchmarks/chapter-plan.md) with separate development and held-out cases, repeated trials for actual models, and cost accounting for feedback calls. Compare against both the original one-shot system and a baseline given the same extra call budget. Otherwise an apparent gain may reflect extra attempts rather than the proposed learning mechanism.

The example's fixed refiner improves its supplied fixtures by construction. Those assertions check the teaching behavior; they do not measure real model improvement. Detailed optimization, continual learning and forgetting belong in the [next deep dive](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/14-learning-and-self-improvement/chapter-plan.md). Operational deployment and recovery follow in [reliability and operations](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/03-building-blocks/15-reliability-and-operations/chapter-plan.md).

### Costs and failure modes

Extra feedback calls add latency and cost. Durable experiences can become stale, while large libraries can make the relevant skill harder to select. A narrow instruction can fix one example and break another. Evaluate changes to the generator, checker and selected package separately, and label unverified feedback as such.

<details><summary>Check your understanding</summary>

An assistant reads an updated `SKILL.md` and handles a new stock task better. No training job ran. Were its model weights updated?

No. The package supplied new instructions at inference time. The application's reusable procedure changed, and its benefit still needs held-out and retention evidence. A weight update requires a separate training mechanism.

</details>

## Security preview

Feedback and reusable experiences become inputs to later decisions. Pass 2 examines misleading feedback and unsafe optimization through [retrieval, memory and data security](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/07-security-by-component-and-workflow-stage/02-retrieval-memory-and-data/chapter-plan.md) and [end-to-end attack paths](https://github.com/RenatoMignone/From-LLMs-to-Secure-Agents/blob/main/knowledge/07-security-by-component-and-workflow-stage/07-end-to-end-attack-paths/chapter-plan.md).

## Key takeaways

- Name the changed object: current context, artifact, memory, instructions, skills or weights.
- Reflection generates a possible explanation; evidence and acceptance checks decide whether a revision works.
- Authored packages and experience-derived code skills are distinct forms of reuse.
- Every claimed improvement needs a baseline, transfer and retention checks, and a rollback path.
